---
title: "Recurrent events: the next event and the number of recurrences"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.6,
  out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 96
)
```

The backward joint model assumes each patient has *one* terminal event. Many
clinical processes do not: a heart-failure patient is discharged, readmitted,
discharged again, and so on, until death or the end of follow-up. This page
shows how to use BJM when events recur, using hospital readmissions and death
as the running example, and answers two questions at a discharge:

| Question | Function |
|---|---|
| Is the **next** event a readmission or a death, and by when? | `predictRisk()` |
| **How many** readmissions will there be in the next 6 months? | `predictRecurrentCount()` |

## The idea: restart the clock at every discharge

Cut each patient's history into **episodes**. An episode starts at a discharge
(time 0 on its own clock) and ends at the next readmission, at death, or when
follow-up stops. Within an episode the situation is exactly the one BJM was
built for: one event, of one of two types, preceded by biomarker
measurements. So an episode is treated as a "patient", with these additions:

* the clock restarts at the discharge, so a readmission's time in hospital is
  *not* time at risk;
* labs drawn during a stay, or before the first discharge, precede the episode
  they help predict and are kept with *negative* times;
* the number of the episode (1st discharge, 2nd, ...) is a covariate, so a
  patient's earlier readmissions inform the later risk.

`buildRecurrentEpisodes()` does the cutting. Everything after it is the
ordinary BJM workflow.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(BJM)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(2026)
```

## Example data

BJM does not ship a recurrent-event data set, so we simulate a small cohort in
the shape your own data would have. The code only makes the example data; skip
to the next section if you have your own.

```{r simulate}
# One patient: time-to-readmission and type depend on age, sex, the number of
# previous readmissions and a patient-level frailty; a biomarker's trajectory
# in each episode depends on how long that episode lasts. Times are in months
# since the first (index) discharge.
simulate_patient <- function(id, follow_up = c(6, 12), max_episodes = 12) {
  age <- rnorm(1, 70, 8); sex <- rbinom(1, 1, 0.5); age_c <- (age - 70) / 10
  frailty <- rnorm(1, 0, 0.5)
  u0 <- rnorm(1, 0, 0.5) + 0.8 * frailty; u1 <- rnorm(1, 0, 0.3)
  end_of_follow_up <- if (is.null(follow_up)) Inf else runif(1, follow_up[1], follow_up[2])
  stay <- function() max(0.08, rexp(1, 1 / 0.25))        # months in hospital

  start <- 0; stay_before <- stay(); k <- 0
  events <- list(); labs <- list(); starts <- numeric(0)
  repeat {
    k <- k + 1; starts[k] <- start
    gap <- (-log(runif(1)) / (0.25 * exp(0.3 * age_c + 0.3 * sex + 0.25 * (k - 1) + frailty)))^(1 / 1.2)
    dies <- rbinom(1, 1, plogis(-2 + 0.5 * gap + 0.3 * age_c + 0.3 * (k - 1)))
    end <- start + gap
    censored <- end > end_of_follow_up
    stop_time <- if (censored) end_of_follow_up else end

    # labs: two in the stay before this discharge, one at discharge, then
    # a visit every half month while the patient is still at risk
    t <- c(start - stay_before * c(0.7, 0.3), start)
    j <- 1
    while (start + 0.5 * j < stop_time) { t <- c(t, start + 0.5 * j); j <- j + 1 }
    mean_lab <- 5 + u0 + (-0.3 + u1) * (t - start) + 0.4 * gap - 0.5 * gap * (t - start) +
      0.05 * age_c + 0.2 * sex
    labs[[k]] <- data.frame(id = id, t = t, biomarker = rnorm(length(t), mean_lab, 0.4))

    row <- function(time, status, discharge = NA_real_)
      data.frame(id = id, time = time, status = status, discharge = discharge, age = age, sex = sex)
    if (censored) { events[[k]] <- row(end_of_follow_up, 0L); break }
    if (dies == 1) { events[[k]] <- row(end, 2L); break }
    next_stay <- stay()
    events[[k]] <- row(end, 1L, discharge = end + next_stay)
    if (end + next_stay >= end_of_follow_up || k >= max_episodes) break
    start <- end + next_stay; stay_before <- next_stay
  }
  list(events = do.call(rbind, events), labs = do.call(rbind, labs), starts = starts)
}

cohort <- lapply(1:300, simulate_patient)
events <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cohort, `[[`, "events"))
labs   <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cohort, `[[`, "labs"))
```

You need two tables.

**`events`: one row per readmission, death or end of follow-up.**

```{r events-head}
head(events[events$id == 1, ], 5)
```

`time` is when the event happened, `status` is `1` for a readmission, `2` for
a death and `0` for the end of follow-up with nothing happening, and
`discharge` is when the stay that a readmission began ends (`NA` when there is
no stay: death, or follow-up ending). Other columns are covariates.

**`labs`: one row per measurement, on the same time axis.**

```{r labs-head}
head(labs[labs$id == 1, ], 5)
```

Times before 0 are labs from the first hospital stay. The picture below shows
what one patient's data looks like once it is cut into episodes.

```{r timeline, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 2.6}
p <- cohort[[1]]
ev <- p$events
n_ep <- nrow(ev)
starts <- p$starts
at_risk <- data.frame(from = starts, to = ev$time, label = paste("Episode", seq_len(n_ep)))
stays <- data.frame(from = c(min(p$labs$t) - 0.15, ev$time[ev$status == 1]),
                    to = c(0, ev$discharge[ev$status == 1]))
last <- ev[n_ep, ]
ink <- "#0b0b0b"; muted <- "#52514e"
ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = stays, aes(xmin = from, xmax = to, ymin = 0.6, ymax = 1.4), fill = "#cfcdc5") +
  geom_rect(data = at_risk, aes(xmin = from, xmax = to, ymin = 0.6, ymax = 1.4), fill = "#2a78d6",
            colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(data = at_risk, aes(x = (from + to) / 2, y = 1, label = label), colour = "white", size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = subset(p$labs, t <= max(ev$time)), aes(x = t, y = 0.2), size = 1.3, colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = stays$from[1], y = 1.65, label = "grey = in hospital (not at risk)",
           colour = muted, size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = stays$from[1], y = -0.15, label = "labs before the first discharge sit in the stay",
           colour = muted, size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  { if (last$status == 0) annotate("text", x = last$time, y = 1.65, label = "end of follow-up",
                                   colour = muted, size = 3, hjust = 1) } +
  { if (last$status == 2) annotate("point", x = last$time, y = 1, shape = 4, size = 4, stroke = 1.3, colour = "#eb6834") } +
  { if (last$status == 2) annotate("text", x = last$time, y = 1.65, label = "death", colour = muted, size = 3) } +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.3, 1.9)) +
  labs(x = "Months since the first discharge", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

## Step 1: cut the history into episodes

```{r build}
built <- buildRecurrentEpisodes(events, labs, time_variable_long = "t",
                                restart_variable = "discharge", lookback = Inf)
```

* `restart_variable = "discharge"` starts each new episode at the discharge
  that ended the stay, not at the readmission. Leave it out when an event takes
  no time (a tumour recurrence, say) and the next episode simply starts at the
  event.
* `lookback = Inf` keeps labs drawn before an episode's start -- in the stay
  before it -- as negative `time_in_episode`, but never reaching back past the
  previous event. The default, `0`, keeps only labs from the start on.

The result has two tables. `episode_data` has one row per episode:

```{r episode-data}
head(built$episode_data[built$episode_data$id == 1, ], 6)
```

`gap` is the length of the episode, `event_any` says whether it ended in an
event (rather than the end of follow-up), `event_type` is `0` for a
readmission and `1` for a death, and `episode` counts the discharges. The
labs, re-clocked, are in `long_data`:

```{r long-data}
head(built$long_data[built$long_data$id == 1,
                     c("id", "episode", "t", "time_in_episode", "gap", "biomarker")], 6)
```

`time_in_episode` is the time since that episode's discharge, negative for
labs in the stay before it. Note that `gap` is `NA` for an episode that has not
ended, which is how the prediction functions below recognise a patient who is
still at risk.

## Step 2: fit

This is the usual two sub-models, fit on episodes instead of patients. The
survival sub-model uses `gap` as the time and `event_any` as the event, with
the episode number as a covariate; the biomarker model is fit on the episodes
that ended in an event, as with `pbc3`.

One choice matters: **group the biomarker model's random effects by episode
(`episode_id`), not by patient (`id`)**. A patient's biomarker level is
generally different at the start of each episode, because the underlying
trajectory keeps moving, so one random effect per patient is the wrong unit;
each episode is its own "subject", as it already is in the survival
sub-model. In a simulation in which the biomarker's current level drives the
risk, grouping by patient left BJM clearly behind a plain logistic regression
on the last lab value (AUC for a readmission within a month 0.65 against
0.75); grouping by episode closed the gap (0.75 against 0.75).

```{r fit}
surv_fit <- survivalSub(built$episode_data, Surv(gap, event_any) ~ age + sex + episode,
                        event_type ~ gap + age + sex + episode)

long_fit <- longitudinalSub(built$long_data[built$long_data$event_any == 1, ],
                            biomarker ~ time_in_episode + age + sex + gap + gap:time_in_episode,
                            ~ time_in_episode | episode_id)
```

## Step 3: describe the patients to predict for

A new patient is described in the same two-table form, up to *now*: their
earlier readmissions, then one last row saying "no event yet as of now", and
their labs so far. Here are three patients who have just been discharged,
two for the first time and one for the second.

```{r new-patients}
history_at_discharge <- function(p, k) {
  now <- p$starts[k]
  ev <- p$events[seq_len(k - 1), ]                       # earlier readmissions
  last <- data.frame(id = p$events$id[1], time = now + 0.001, status = 0L, discharge = NA_real_,
                     age = p$events$age[1], sex = p$events$sex[1])
  list(events = rbind(ev, last), labs = p$labs[p$labs$t <= now, ])
}

set.seed(7)
fresh <- lapply(5001:5040, simulate_patient, follow_up = NULL)
reach2 <- Filter(function(p) length(p$starts) >= 2, fresh)      # patients with a 2nd discharge
chosen <- list(
  list(p = fresh[[1]], k = 1), list(p = fresh[[2]], k = 1), list(p = reach2[[1]], k = 2))
histories <- lapply(chosen, function(x) history_at_discharge(x$p, x$k))
for (i in seq_along(histories)) {                        # give each prediction its own id
  histories[[i]]$events$id <- histories[[i]]$labs$id <- 9000 + i
}
now_events <- do.call(rbind, lapply(histories, `[[`, "events"))
now_labs   <- do.call(rbind, lapply(histories, `[[`, "labs"))

now <- buildRecurrentEpisodes(now_events, now_labs, time_variable_long = "t",
                              restart_variable = "discharge", lookback = Inf)
# each patient's last episode is the one still open
open <- now$long_data[now$long_data$episode == ave(now$long_data$episode, now$long_data$id, FUN = max), ]
head(open[, c("episode_id", "t", "time_in_episode", "gap", "biomarker", "event_type")], 4)
```

The open episode's `gap` and `event_type` are `NA`, as they must be: what
happens in it is what we are predicting. Each `episode_id` appears
once, so each prediction is its own "subject"; if you want predictions for the
same patient at several discharges, give each its own `id` (the discharges
here already differ in `episode`, but the ids you pass in should not repeat).

## Step 4: the next event

`predictRisk()` is used exactly as before. `prediction_time = 0` is the
discharge; if you predict some time after it, give the time elapsed since the
discharge, and include the labs up to then.

```{r predict-risk}
risk <- predictRisk(open, long_fit, surv_fit, prediction_time = 0, horizon = 1,
                    time_variable = "time_in_episode",
                    survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
round(data.frame(readmission = risk$risk_prob_1, death = risk$risk_prob_2), 3)
```

These are the probabilities that the *next* event happens within a month and
is a readmission, or a death. A longer `horizon` gives, for instance, the
probability of at least one readmission in 3 months.

## Step 5: the number of readmissions

`predictRecurrentCount()` simulates each patient forward, episode by episode,
and counts. The first episode is drawn given the patient's labs (the same
distribution `predictRisk()` uses); later ones are drawn from the model given
the patient's covariates, with the episode number advanced. BJM has no model
of how long a stay lasts, so you supply observed stay lengths, which are
resampled.

```{r predict-count}
stay_lengths <- with(events, discharge[status == 1] - time[status == 1])
count <- predictRecurrentCount(open, long_fit, surv_fit, prediction_time = 0, horizon = 6,
                               time_variable = "time_in_episode", stay_lengths = stay_lengths,
                               n_sim = 400, max_stages = 30, seed = 1)
count
```

The simulated mortality here is far higher than in real heart failure, so
read the output as a format, not as clinical numbers. `count$summary` has the expected number of readmissions, the probability of at
least one or two, and the probability of dying in the window; `count$counts`
holds every simulated path if you want a different summary. The figure shows
the whole distribution for each patient.

```{r count-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3}
s <- count$summary
dist <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s)), function(i) data.frame(
  patient = sprintf("Patient %s\nexpected %.1f, P(death) %.0f%%", s[[1]][i], s$mean_count[i], 100 * s$p_death[i]),
  n = factor(c("0", "1", "2", "3+"), levels = c("0", "1", "2", "3+")),
  p = unlist(s[i, c("p_count_0", "p_count_1", "p_count_2", "p_count_3plus")]))))
ggplot(dist, aes(n, p)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6", width = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ patient, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Readmissions in the next 6 months", y = "Probability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "#0b0b0b"))
```

## Things to watch for

* **Time units.** Use one unit throughout (here months). `horizon`, the labs'
  times and `stay_lengths` must all be in it.
* **`max_stages`.** Paths are stopped after this many episodes; the function
  warns, and sets `count$capped`, when that happens. Raise it for long
  windows or high-risk patients.
* **Covariates that change by episode.** The episode number is advanced for
  you. If your survival model uses other episode-specific covariates, such
  as the length of the previous gap, pass `next_covariates = function(row, k)`
  to update them.
* **The outcome columns must exist** in the prediction data. When it comes
  from `buildRecurrentEpisodes()` they do (as `NA`); if you build it by hand,
  add them.

## What this assumes, and what it has been checked against

* Within an episode, the model is the backward joint model, and carries its
  assumptions. Across episodes, patients are linked only through their
  covariates and the episode number: **only the first step of the count
  prediction uses the patient's biomarkers**, and a patient-level tendency to
  recur that is not in the covariates (a frailty) is not carried forward.
* The stay length is resampled from the data, independently of everything
  else.
* The survival sub-model treats a patient's episodes as independent. Its
  coefficients are still estimates of the gap-time model, but the standard
  errors in `summary(surv_fit)` ignore the correlation between a patient's
  episodes and are too small.
* Checks so far are simulations (kept outside the package): ordinary BJM with one discharge per patient; several
  hospitalizations per patient, with and without a patient-level frailty; and
  the count prediction. In them, the predicted probabilities of the next event
  and the expected counts were close to the truth, and ranked patients better
  than logistic and Poisson regressions on the last lab value. A frailty
  weakened the next-event predictions (calibration slopes fell from about 0.95
  to 0.75-0.90). A joint frailty model from the `frailtypack` package, which
  uses event history but no biomarkers, ranked patients much worse; a
  frailty model *with* biomarkers (`trivPenal()`) could not be compared, as it
  was too slow and does not fit labs measured afresh at each discharge.
  The simulated disease is not calibrated to any real one.
* Nothing here has been checked on real data.
